div.div:
Why invalidate-on-deny matters (the RQ4 lesson)
A compromised device first tries lateral movement and breaker commands. Those are denied, and each denial lowers its trust at the PDP until even its telemetry would be denied. A naive cache keeps serving the old telemetry allow and so bypasses the trust decay. Dropping all cached entries of a subject on any deny closes that gap for the cost of one extra PDP round trip.

text.tspan: Why invalidate-on-deny matters (the RQ4 lesson)
A compromised device first tries lateral movement and breaker commands. Those
are denied, and each denial lowers its trust at the PDP until even its telemetry
would be denied. A naive cache keeps serving the old telemetry allow and so
bypasses the trust decay. Dropping all cached entries of a subject on any deny
closes that gap for the cost of one extra PDP round trip.

div.div: General rule: every cache in a zero-trust system must be invalidated by trust changes, not only by policy and revocation events. Next step: a per-subject trust epoch pushed by the PDP.

div.div:
Staleness budget
unauthorized window = detection delay + signal transport + cache staleness. Cache staleness ≤ min(TTL, revocation poll interval). Short TTLs on dangerous actions keep the worst case small.

text.tspan: Staleness budget
unauthorized window = detection delay + signal transport + cache staleness. Cache staleness ≤ min(TTL, revocation poll interval). Short TTLs on dangerous actions keep
the worst case small.

div.b: Design choice: pull, not push (for now)

ul.li: polling an epoch is one tiny GET, works through NAT and the DMZ, and degrades gracefully during a partition (the PEP knows it is stale)
push (server-sent events) would cut the window to the network delay; noted for later
